meta.title: A stranger at the shop’s door
meta.line: Predict: what should the shop ask this agent first?
meta.caption: You ask your personal AI agent to exchange a jacket at example.com. The shop has never met this agent, and the agent has no way in yet. It could borrow your password and pass as you, or arrive as an anonymous bot and be turned away. Poppy, the Personal Agent Protocol, is a third way. What would you want the shop to ask first?

meta.title: First, the shop says how to reach it
meta.line: One file lists the ways in.
meta.caption: The agent fetches example.com/.well-known/poppy.json. The file lists the ways in: the shop’s APIs, its website, its own agent to chat with, and the page where sign-in happens. The agent checks that the file speaks for the domain that served it, so a copy on another site cannot send it elsewhere. Four lanes now run between the agent and the Company, as Poppy calls the shop.

meta.title: The agent seals what it sends
meta.line: The seal says which agent is asking, and for which User.
meta.caption: The agent adds a medium to the cart. The request carries a Session header, drawn as the wax seal, signed with the agent’s published keys. The Company now knows the agent, a User ID and a Session for the cart. The User ID is a pseudonym made for this Company, so the shop still does not know you. Your agent signs every request to say who is asking, and you approve separately what it may do with your account.

meta.title: One Session, three lanes
meta.line: The website and the chat join the same Session.
meta.caption: The same seal works on each lane. The agent’s browser joins the Session with a one-time code, so the website sees the same visitor and the same cart. In the chat, the Company’s own agent answers a question about sizes, and each message says whether a person or an AI wrote it. Look at what the Company knows: the Session has not changed.

meta.title: A seal is not a key
meta.line: Exchange refused: 401, it needs orders:write.
meta.caption: Now the errand itself. The exchange would change order 1042, so the request stops short of the Company: 401, naming the permission it needs, orders:write. A Session header never grants account access, whatever it says. That takes a second proof, and the agent cannot make that one for itself.

meta.title: You hand over a key, not your password
meta.line: Standard OAuth, on the Company’s own page.
meta.caption: The agent sends you to the Company’s sign-in page. You sign in there and approve orders:read and orders:write. The Company gives the agent an access token, drawn as a key with one tooth for each scope you approved. Your password stays with you, and the Company can take this one key back without locking you out. Sign-in does not mention the Session: what the Company knows has not changed.

meta.title: Seal and key together
meta.line: 200: the exchange is made.
meta.caption: The same request now carries both, and the Company joins them: this Session may act on your account, within orders:read and orders:write. The exchange is made. The seal also covers the key, so the Company can tell that the agent holding the key is the agent that signed.

answer.reason: the access token was issued to another agent

meta.title: A stolen key will not turn
meta.line: 400 invalid_session: the key belongs to another seal.
meta.caption: Suppose a thief copies the key. It has to send it under a seal of its own, and the Company sees a key issued to agent.example arriving under another agent’s seal: 400 invalid_session. What the Company knows does not change. A whole request copied in transit could be replayed to the same address for a short time, which is why the agent signs a fresh seal for each request.

meta.title: Take the key back, keep the Session
meta.line: Now drive it yourself: a refused press says why.
meta.caption: The agent gives up its token, and account access ends. The Session carries on, with the same User ID and the same cart. Press the events to drive the protocol yourself, and read why a refused press is refused. One limit: Poppy binds agents that choose to follow it. An agent that types your password into the website looks like you, and the Company cannot tell.

meta.title: Turned back at the counter
meta.line: Predict: what should your agent do next?
meta.caption: Your agent sends the jacket exchange from chapter 1, with its seal and its key. This morning the Company turns the ticket back with a slip: 401 invalid_token, about the key. The key expired overnight. The agent could send it again, start a new Session, or ask you to sign in. Which would you do? The slip already says.

meta.title: The slip says what to bring
meta.line: invalid_token: refresh the key, send it again.
meta.caption: The agent trades its refresh token for a new access token, without asking you, and sends the same request: 200, the exchange is made. Each refusal’s code names its own remedy, and the agent applies that one: the wrong one loops, or throws away a good token. Had you disconnected the agent from your account, the refresh would fail, and the agent would carry on signed out.

meta.title: A key cut for reading
meta.line: 403 names the scope; you approve it again.
meta.caption: Suppose you had approved only orders:read. The slip says 403 insufficient_scope, naming orders:write. A refresh gives no more than you approved, so the agent asks you to sign in again, for orders:read and orders:write together. A 401 with no code, sent with no key at all, is handled the same way, unless you signed out: then the agent waits for you to ask.

meta.title: When the seal itself is wrong
meta.line: 400 invalid_session: fix the cause. A new Session won’t.
meta.caption: Now the number changes. The delegation that vouches for the agent’s signing key has expired, and the slip says 400 invalid_session, about the seal. A new Session would carry the same broken seal and be refused the same way. So the agent stops, gets a new delegation, signs again in the same Session, and sends. The cart is still there.

meta.title: Why a seal’s error is not a 401
meta.line: A 401 would make OAuth code discard a good key.
meta.caption: OAuth libraries read a 401 as “this token is bad” and throw the token away. Had the Company answered the expired delegation with 401, the agent’s library would have discarded a key that was fine, and the agent would have refreshed, or asked you to sign in, for nothing. Poppy sends Session errors as 400, so the key stays where it is.

meta.title: The Session is over
meta.line: session_ended: a new Session, and one more try.
meta.caption: The Company has ended the Session the cart was in. The slip says 400 session_ended, so the agent starts a new Session and sends the exchange again, once. The cart stays behind with the old Session. Had the new Session been refused the same way, the agent would have stopped there: without that rule, agent and Company could pass the request back and forth for ever.

meta.title: Same 400, a different move
meta.line: version_unsupported: read poppy.json again, then choose.
meta.caption: Third 400, third remedy. The agent used an old copy of poppy.json and sent version 0.4, which the Company no longer serves. It fetches poppy.json again, uncached, chooses 1.0, and, since a Session keeps one version, starts a new Session and sends once more. The extensions a request declares work the same way: a 403 extension_required names the one missing. Read the code, not just the number.

meta.title: A key cut for one door
meta.line: The MCP server takes only keys issued for it.
meta.caption: A Company can list two kinds of API: an OpenAPI service and an MCP server. Both take the seal and the key. This MCP server accepts only tokens issued for it, so the everyday key comes back 401 invalid_token, with a link to the server’s metadata. The agent refreshes for a token whose resource is the server’s URL, and uses that token there and nowhere else.

meta.title: Slow down, then break it yourself
meta.line: Break the errand, then predict how the agent answers.
meta.caption: Send too fast and the Company answers 429 with Retry-After: 30. The key and the seal are fine, so the agent waits at least 30 seconds and sends the same request. Now it is yours. Break the errand one of seven ways, say which remedy you expect, then press Agent answers. The rail shows the remedy, and why the tempting one, New Session here, would fail.

meta.title: A seal from a stranger
meta.line: Predict: why should the shop believe this seal?
meta.caption: Your agent sends example.com the jacket exchange, sealed as in chapter 1. The shop has never met this agent and shares no secret with it. Still it must learn which agent sent this and which User it is for, without learning who that User is. Each line on the ticket is a claim the seal makes. What would make a copy of this seal useless to anyone else?

meta.title: The sender’s name is an address
meta.line: iss is a URL that returns the agent’s keys.
meta.caption: Inside the seal, a claim called iss names the agent as a URL, https://agent.example/agent.json, and the shop fetches it. The document there must give that same URL as its client_id, and it lists the agent’s published keys on the same domain. Anyone can claim to be agent.example. Only agent.example decides which keys hang at that address.

meta.title: The published key never touches a request
meta.line: It signs a short pass; the pass’s key seals.
meta.caption: Three links: the agent's URL publishes its keys, one vouches for a short-lived key, and that key seals each request. The published key signs a delegation: a pass lasting at most 24 hours, this one until 06:00, naming a delegated key and nothing about you or the shop. That key presses a fresh seal for each request. So the key all shops trust records nowhere which shops you use. Two signatures and an address: three links.

meta.title: Punched in order
meta.line: All 11 checks hold, two of them optional.
meta.caption: The shop walks the chain from iss down to the seal, then the claims: typed as a Session JWT, addressed to this shop, for this method and URL, signed a second ago, covering the token it carries. Then two optional checks: a jti it has not seen, and a key that has signed for no other User. 200. Some agents also sign for the network edge with Web Bot Auth; that replaces none of this.

meta.title: Your agent opens a conversation
meta.line: Predict: where will the shop’s reply come from?
meta.caption: Your agent wants to exchange the jacket from order 1042, so it talks with example.com’s own agent: JSON over HTTPS, signed with its Session header as chapter 1 showed. Its first message starts the conversation. The answer is 201 with a Conversation ID, cnv_8f3Kd2, and no reply: the Company has accepted the message, not answered it, so working is true. Where will the reply come from?

meta.title: Replies are read, not returned
meta.line: Read until working is false.
meta.caption: The agent reads the conversation’s events from where it last stopped, or holds the read open, or streams it. The reply is an event, and it says who wrote it: here an AI. Every message says whether a person or an AI wrote it, on both sides, and only your own agent can bring you in. A request lost on the way is safe to send again with the same request ID: the Company acts on it once. Try the controls here to request a person, invite the User and open a Direct Conversation.

meta.title: A person takes the empty seat
meta.line: Pending, then a person joins: responder is human.
meta.caption: The agent asks for a person. Handoff turns pending while the Company looks, and its agent keeps answering meanwhile, so responder stays agent. When Alex joins, handoff is none again, responder is human, and Alex’s reply carries the person mark. Had nobody been free, handoff would go back to none and the Company Agent would say why. A cancel may not take effect, so the agent watches these fields.

meta.title: The Company asks for you
meta.line: Predict: can the Company bring you in itself?
meta.caption: Alex wants to confirm the exchange with you, not with your agent. The Company cannot reach you. It can only add a user_requested event to the conversation, with a short reason, and none of the four fields changes. The invitation lands in front of your agent, which asks you whether you want to talk. What happens if you say no?

meta.title: A second, smaller table
meta.line: Only your agent can open it.
meta.caption: You agree, so your agent opens a Direct Conversation: a new conversation, linked to the first, where you speak for yourself and your agent may watch. The Company keeps the earlier history, and you need not read it. Had you said no, your agent would have told the Company for you. While the small table is open, the first one waits: a message there gets 409 direct_conversation_open.

meta.title: Your own words are marked human
meta.line: The same words from your agent would be marked AI.
meta.caption: You type “Medium, please.” and your agent sends it as written, marked human. Had your agent passed on your wish in its own words, as a summary, the message would be marked agent: only your own words count as yours. The specialist’s reply carries the person mark too, so all four voices stay distinct. Draft 1.0 adds that either side reads a mark it does not know as AI, so nothing passes for a person’s words unless it says human.

meta.title: Who may continue this conversation
meta.line: A mismatch looks like no conversation at all.
meta.caption: Suppose the Company Agent had needed your account. It adds an authorization event; your agent signs you in and carries on in the same conversation with an access token. From then on the conversation belongs to agent.example, User ID usr_Q7c1vK and account A, whatever Session asks. Signed out, the agent gets a challenge to sign in again. Another User ID, or account B, gets 404, as if it did not exist.

meta.title: The small table closes, the big one listens
meta.line: Now drive both sides yourself: refusals say why.
meta.caption: You are done, so your agent closes the Direct Conversation, and the first conversation takes messages again. A close does not wait its turn: the Company may drop anything it has not acted on yet, so the agent reads until working is false before it closes. Closing does not cancel the exchange itself. Now press the events, for both sides, and read why a refused press is refused. To repeat the handoff and invitation, return to “Replies are read, not returned”.

Poppy tells an agent to read the shop’s task list before it starts; this one skipped it. What would the list have said? Try “Read the shop’s list” here, or continue through the explanation.

meta.title: Anyone can write a poppy.json
meta.line: Predict: how would you forge one?
meta.caption: Your agent is about to shop at www.example.com. In chapter 1 its first move was to read the shop’s poppy.json, a file that tells it where to send your requests and your tokens. But a JSON file is the easiest thing on the web to forge. Before you go on, think how you would make an agent believe that a file of yours speaks for example.com.

meta.title: The file speaks for the host that served it
meta.line: It must name that host itself.
meta.caption: The agent fetches www.example.com/.well-known/poppy.json over HTTPS, and the shop redirects it to the same path on example.com, which is allowed. The file lists the ways in, at least one of them: the shop’s APIs, its website and its own agent, beside sign-in details, tasks and extensions. Its letterhead, organization.domain, says example.com, and the agent checks that this is the host that served it.

meta.title: A handshake with the issuer
meta.line: The domain names its issuer; the issuer names it back.
meta.caption: Who issues this shop’s tokens? example.com’s protected resource metadata, the signpost, names auth.example.com. The agent then asks the issuer, whose own metadata lists example.com among its domains. Each side points at the other, and from now on the Company is known by its issuer. That is the answer: The domain names its issuer and the issuer lists the domain back, and each check stops one way to impersonate the shop. Three forgers now try to get round one check each.

meta.title: A copy on a lookalike domain
meta.line: Refused: it names example.com, not examp1e.com.
meta.caption: The first forger copies example.com’s file to examp1e.com and points the API address at its own server. The file is at the right path, over HTTPS, but it still says example.com and examp1e.com served it, so the agent refuses it at the domain check. Change the letterhead to examp1e.com and every check passes, even under example.com’s name and logo (draft 1.0, 10.3). The file then speaks for examp1e.com, a different Company, and noticing that domain falls to the agent.

meta.title: Claiming the shop’s issuer
meta.line: The issuer does not list evil.example.
meta.caption: A cleverer forger is honest about its domain. evil.example serves a file naming evil.example, and its signpost names auth.example.com as its issuer. Believe that, and evil.example is the same Company as example.com: the agent would send it example.com’s User ID and tokens. But the issuer’s own register does not list evil.example. The handshake is missing its second side, and the agent refuses the file.

meta.title: A file uploaded to the real shop
meta.line: The path check alone stops it.
meta.caption: The cleverest forger uploads a file naming example.com to example.com itself, at /uploads/poppy.json, and redirects deals.example’s well-known address to it. The file is served by example.com and names example.com, and example.com’s issuer lists example.com, so every other check would pass. The path check stops it: a redirect may go to any host, but it must end at /.well-known/poppy.json. Whoever controls that path speaks for the shop.

meta.title: A shop with no issuer
meta.line: Signed out: the domain is the Company.
meta.caption: Some shops run no sign-in. corner.example’s metadata answers 404, which means it has no issuer, so there is no listing to ask for. The Company is then known by its own address, https://corner.example, and the agent can use it in signed-out Sessions only. Without an issuer, each domain is a Company of its own.

meta.title: An error is not “no issuer”
meta.line: The agent stops rather than fall back.
meta.caption: Today example.com’s metadata times out. A careless agent would treat that like corner.example’s 404 and carry on with https://example.com as the Company. That would change the Company’s identifier, and with it the User ID the agent uses there. So after a timeout, an error status or invalid metadata the agent never falls back to the domain: it stops.

meta.title: Two domains, one Company
meta.line: Now choose who serves the file.
meta.caption: example.co.uk serves its own file and names the same issuer, which lists it too. So it is the same Company as example.com, with the same User ID, Sessions and refresh tokens. Each file also states its protocol version; the agent sends the one it chose as Poppy-Version, and a shop that no longer serves it answers 400 version_unsupported. Choose who serves the file and run the checks.
